I could begin with an apology or a confession. A thousand words is not very many. It is also, depending on the day, far too many. The blank space expects something, and I am supposed to fill it with language, as if language were water and the page a glass. But the glass is already full of everything I have not said, the silences between people, the half-formed thoughts that never make it to speech, the small gestures that do the work of paragraphs. If I had a thousand words, I might spend them asking what a word is worth.

A word is a small unit of attention. It is a sound or a mark that stands in for a thing, an idea, a feeling. It is also a commitment. To say a word is to choose one possibility over countless others. In this sentence, I chose "countless" instead of "many" or "infinite" or "unnumbered." Each choice closes doors. A thousand words is a thousand closures, a thousand small deaths of alternative expression. That sounds dramatic, but writing is dramatic. Even when it is quiet, it is a performance of thought.

What would I do with a thousand words if I did not have to worry about being interesting or coherent? I might list the objects on my desk: a ceramic mug with a hairline crack, a stack of books with broken spines, a pair of scissors, a pencil with no eraser, a receipt from a grocery store I do not remember visiting. The receipt says "bananas, oats, dish soap, dark chocolate." That is four words, but they summon a whole morning: the fluorescent lights, the squeak of a cart wheel, the decision to buy chocolate even though it was not on the list. Lists are a form of attention. They say: this existed, I noticed it, it mattered enough to name.

But a thousand words can also be a container for a story. Here is a story: A woman walks into a library and asks for a book she read as a child. She does not remember the title or the author. She remembers only that the cover was blue and there was a fox on it, and the fox was wearing a small red scarf. The librarian, who has heard this before, smiles and walks to a shelf. She pulls down a book with a blue cover and a fox in a red scarf. "This one?" she asks. The woman begins to cry. Not because the book is the right one, but because someone believed her memory enough to look. That story is not true, but it is true in the way that stories are true: it is about recognition, about being seen, about the small miracle of a specific detail surviving the blur of years. I used about ninety words to tell it. I have nine hundred and ten left.

I could use them to describe the weather. It is raining here, or maybe it is not raining where you are. Rain is a convenient subject because it is both ordinary and full of metaphor. Rain is sorrow, renewal, inconvenience, music. The word "rain" itself is small and plain, but it contains the sound of water on leaves, the smell of wet pavement, the gray light of an overcast afternoon, the memory of a canceled picnic, the relief of a drought ending. A thousand words could be spent entirely on rain and still not exhaust it. But I will not do that. I will mention the rain only to say that it is there, in the background, like the hum of a refrigerator or the distant sound of traffic. Background noise is also a kind of language. It says the world is still running.

What else? I could write about fear. Fear is a word that is used so often it has become smooth, like a stone in a river. But fear is not smooth when it arrives. It is jagged. It is the 3 a.m. thought that will not be put away. It is the phone ringing at an unusual hour. It is the moment after you say something true and before the other person responds. A thousand words might be enough to walk around fear, to see its shape from different angles, to notice that it is often protecting something tender. But I do not want to spend all my words on fear. It has had enough attention already.

I could write about love. Love is even harder than fear because it has been sung and shouted and whispered and written on bathroom walls. Love is a word that carries the weight of every love that has ever been spoken, and so it is always both too large and too small. If I say "I love you," I mean something specific, but the words are general. They are a container, and the listener must fill them with context. Maybe that is why we say it so often, to keep filling the container, to keep the meaning from evaporating. A thousand words of love would still not be enough, but it might be a beginning.

I could write about writing. That is what I am doing, after all. Writing about writing is like a mirror facing a mirror. It can go on forever, but it can also be a way of finding out what I think. I do not always know what I think until I watch the words appear. This is not a mystical process. It is more like walking in the dark with a small flashlight. The beam only reaches a few feet ahead, but that is enough to take the next step. A thousand words is a thousand steps. Some of them will be in the wrong direction. That is all right. The point is to keep walking.

I have twenty-two words left. I will spend them on this: look at the ordinary world. It is full of small, luminous things. Please notice them now.
